turns.prompt_text: I've got this bop it with me and I see that the Muppet extreme is very expensive
turns.response_html:
It is wild how much some of these old handheld games are going for now. If you're looking at the Bop It Extreme or Extreme 2, the "expensive" tags usually come down to a mix of nostalgia and the fact that these specific models were the peak of the series for many people.

While you might see some ambitious listings for hundreds of dollars, the actual market value is usually a bit more grounded. Here is the breakdown of what people are paying in 2026:

Current Market Value

ModelConditionTypical Price
Bop It Extreme (1998)Used (Tested)$30 – $50
Bop It Extreme 2 (2002)Used (Tested)$35 – $45
Any Extreme ModelBrand New (Sealed)$150 – $200+

Why is it so pricey?

  • The "Gold Standard" Mechanics: The Extreme versions added the Spin It and Flick It commands, making them the most complex and satisfying versions to play compared to the simpler modern "button" versions.
  • Durability Issues: These toys were built for kids to bash around. Finding one where the "Spin It" wheel hasn't seized up or the "Flick It" lever hasn't snapped is becoming harder.
  • Collector Nostalgia: For people in their late 20s and 30s, this is a prime "childhood" relic. Sealed units are treated as museum pieces by collectors.

Pro-Tip for Buying or Selling

If you're checking prices on sites like eBay, make sure to filter by "Sold Items" rather than just active listings. People often list them for $200+, but they rarely actually sell for that unless they are in the original box.

If yours is working and in good shape, it’s definitely a solid little piece of tech history to have!

turns.prompt_text: I imagine it would not be too difficult to 3D print a replica or similar model and hook up some electronics
turns.response_html:
It is surprisingly feasible to build a replica, especially since the "complex" mechanical actions are actually quite simple from an electronics standpoint.

The Mechanical Reality

Teardowns of the Extreme models show that every action (Twist It, Pull It, Flick It, Spin It) essentially just triggers a standard momentary push button on the internal control board.

  • Flick It/Pull It: These usually use a spring-loaded lever that physically depresses a button when moved.
  • Spin It: This often uses a wheel with a "cam" or a notched internal edge that clicks a button as it rotates.
  • Bop It: A simple center plunger over a tactile switch.

3D Printing Strategy

Since you're already familiar with prototyping from low-fidelity to high-fidelity, you could iterate on the mechanical feel before committing to a full assembly.

  • Existing Files: There are already replacement STL files for the "Spin It" wheel and "Flick It" lever on platforms like Thingiverse and Printables. You could use these as a foundation for the mechanical interfaces.
  • Filament Choice: * PLA/PETG for the main housing.
    • TPU could be interesting for the "Bop It" button or the grips to give it that rubberized, tactile feel of the original.
  • The "Click": The hardest part to replicate is the specific "snap" and spring tension. You’d likely want to source some generic compression springs and high-quality tactile switches (like Omron or even mechanical keyboard switches for a "premium" Bop It).

The Brains (Electronics)

An Arduino Nano or an ESP32 would be more than enough to handle the logic.

  • Logic: A simple state machine that picks a random action, plays an audio file, and waits for the corresponding GPIO pin to go HIGH within a decreasing time window.
  • Audio: You could use a DFPlayer Mini to trigger MP3 samples of the original voice (easily found in soundboard archives).
  • Expansion: If you use an ESP32, you could technically add a web-based leaderboard or even Bluetooth multiplayer.

Note on the "Extreme" complexity: The original used a custom COB (Chip-on-Board) that handled the audio and timing. Replicating the logic in C++ or MicroPython is a great afternoon project.
